newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Ramos acts to end Philippine budget row.
newsitem.headline: Ramos acts to end Philippine budget row.

text.p: Philippine President Fidel Ramos summoned Congress to a two-day special session starting on Monday to pass the 1997 national budget after political bickerings stalled its approval.
Ramos announced the session in an armed forces day speech on Sunday where he pledged to raise the pay of 1.3 million civil servants, including 107,500 soldiers, effective on New Year's Day.
"This is one of the strongest reasons why I decided to call a special session of Congress for two days," he said.
The two-chamber Congress adjourned on Thursday for a one-month break without passing the budget after squabbling over a proposed 1.2-billion-peso ($46 million) countrywide development fund (CDF).
The CDF is for use by legislators to fund projects in their respective areas but newspapers say it has been misused.

Deliberations hit an impasse after the opposition-led Senate slashed the fund by 40 percent to 720 million pesos ($28 million). Senate finance committee chief Ernesto Herrera said senators feared the fund, backed by the House of Representatives, could be used for campaigning.
The Philippines is to hold presidential and congressional elections in May 1998. Unofficial campaigning starts early, up to a year before the polls.

"The 1997 budget is the election budget," the Manila Standard said on Sunday. "The projects initiated in 1997 will define, in the eyes of the voters, the performance of their elected representatives as the 1998 election season comes around."
House Speaker Jose de Venecia, a potential presidential aspirant, told Ramos on Sunday it would be difficult to reconcile the differences over the CDF but "Congress will try its best".
The Lower House has proposed a 479.9 billion pesos ($18.4 billion) budget and the Senate 392.3 billion pesos ($15 billion).
Failure of the special session to pass the budget would not automatically paralyse government. Under the law, it can use the previous year's budget until Congress approves a new one.
